Debt Crisis Grips Zimbabwe’s Engineering & Construction Industry

Zimbabwe’s Engineering & Construction industry is in the grip of a mounting debt crisis, with companies halting projects and thousands of workers facing uncertainty as the sector struggles to stay afloat. The crisis, triggered by a sudden contraction in credit availability last month, has forced many firms to suspend operations at key construction sites across Harare, Bulawayo, and Mutare.

Industry insiders report that the freeze in lending began abruptly after several major engineering firms failed to refinance maturing loans. “We had anticipated a renewal of our credit facility, but banks have completely closed their doors to new lending for now,” said Tawanda Chikore, chief financial officer at ZimPro Engineering. “Work on three of our sites has stopped, and we’ve had to send home over 200 skilled workers without pay.”

The Zimbabwe Association of Engineering & Construction Companies estimates that at least 60% of medium and large contractors have made similar workforce reductions in the past two weeks. “It’s a perfect storm,” said association president Edith Gondo. “Spiraling debt, frozen credit lines, and evaporating cash flow have brought many projects to a standstill. We are deeply concerned for the livelihoods of our workforce.”

Several high-profile projects, including bridges, public buildings, and private developments, are now on hold. At the sprawling New Horizons site in eastern Harare, dozens of unfinished concrete frames sit idle. Workers, some of whom had travelled from rural areas for employment, have been left stranded. “I don’t know when I’ll be called back,” said John Moyo, a foreman who has worked in the industry for 15 years. “Many of us are just waiting, hoping the situation changes.”

Analysts warn the crisis could deepen if firms are unable to restructure their debts. “The sector’s balance sheets were already fragile due to delayed payments and rising material costs,” said Tatenda Mlauzi, an independent construction sector analyst. “With the credit freeze, even previously healthy companies are now unable to meet payroll or service their debts.”

The Engineering & Construction Industry Workers Union has called for urgent intervention. “If nothing is done, we could see mass redundancies,” said union secretary-general Memory Ncube. “Our members and their families are at risk.”

As the crisis continues, uncertainty hangs over the future of Zimbabwe’s engineering and construction sector, with no immediate relief in sight.
